newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PRESS DIGEST - Australian General News - August 1.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Australian General News - August 1.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

New South Wales Premier Bob Carr yesterday announced a coronial inquest into the landslide at Thredbo which trapped about 20 people in the Carinya Lodge and the Bimbadeen Lodge. Police said there was little hope of finding life, after heat and sound seeking equipment did not show any sign of survivors. Page 1.

The states will oppose the Federal Government's cost-conscious plan for a five-year Medicare agreement covering A$5 billion of annual funding for public hospitals. The full details of the funding deal will not be available to the States until next year, but it is likely to include a case mix funding formula. Page 3.

Four national contractors have agreed to a wage rise of 13.5 percent over the next 27 months and other employment entitlements for construction unions involved in their West Australian projects. The settlements in Western Australia will set benchmarks for upcoming collective bargaining negotiations in the rest of Australia. Page 3.

An immediate call for a Bill of Rights to be included in the Australian Constitution via referendum followed the High Court's decision on the Kruger case, involving the Aboriginal "stolen children". The court found the Constitution did not protect the rigts of citizens affected by the Government's laws. Page 5.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Rescuers worked throughout the night in a search for survivors of the Thredbo landslide which swept away two ski lodges, burying 20 people. The first body was removed yesterday evening but police said it could be two days before they recover all those who were in the lodges, who include at least 11 men and seven women. Page 1.

A number of geologists and engineers say the most likely explanation for the landslide at Thredbo was that water weakened the slope's stability, which may already have been compromised by the building of roads and chalets. Others say natural erosion or brittle rock may have been responsible. Page 3.

The High Court ruled on the Kruger challenge yesterday that the law allowing the separation of Aboriginal children from their mothers in the Northern Territory until the late 1950s did not authorise genocide, and was valid. The court ruled that Aborigineswere not directly entitled to a damages action even if their Constitutional rights had been violated. Page 5.

A meeting of Federal, State and Territory health, police and justice ministers yesterday voted in favour of the first stage of an ACT trial which would provide heroin to registered users and evaluate new treatments. Only Queensland, Western Australia and he Northern Territory opposed the trial. Australia must now seek approval from the United Nations, with the earliest possible start date for the trial being next July. Page 5.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Thermal imaging and audio probes could not find any evidence of life last night under the rubble of the two Thredbo ski lodges which collapsed under a landslide late Wednesday. Police said hopes of finding any survivors were fading as time passed and temperatures fell. One body was recovered last night, and police fear there may be as many as 19 others. Page 1.

Booking agents and tour operators were concerned yesterday about a possible boycott of Thredbo in favour of other skiing fields, following the landslide which swept away two ski lodges on Wednesday. There had already been many inquiries from people concerned about the safety of Thredbo. Page 3.

Senior New South Wales public servant Roger West said yesterday the Carr Government was preventing the Community Services Commission from investigating problems with homes for children and the disabled by starving the service of funds. West said the servie had received only a quarter of a recommended funding increase and had been forced to let suspected child abuse go uninvestigated. Page 5.

The Newcastle Supreme Court yesterday found former boxing champion Dean Waters not guilty of the murder or manslaughter of horse trainer Allen Hall in 1988. Waters had admitted to police that he and another man had shot Hall, but pleaded diminished responsibility. Page 5.
THE AGE

Rescuers had to wait ten hours yesterday before being allowed to begin the search for survivors at the Thredbo ski lodge disaster, with the fear that the ground would give way again. Pieces of debris were being removed by hand in a human chain as the search continued into the night, with hopes fading. Page 1.

Thredbo locals have criticised the 10-hour delay in beginning the search for people trapped under rubble after Wednesday night's landslide, as cries for help could be heard from under the rubble immediately after the landslide. Police and rescue workers waited for a geophysicist before commencing the search, fearing the site was too unstable. Page A3.

The High Court yesterday unanimously ruled that the laws permitting the removal of Aboriginal children did not constitute genocide and were not unconstitutional. The Court ruled that the "stolen generation" should not receive compensation. Page A6.

The High Court has ruled that public safety is more important than the implied Constitutional right to political protest, banning conservationists from breaking rules when they protest against duck shooters when the hunting season begins. The Court unanimously dismissed the arguments of the Coalition Against Duck Shooting and upheld the Victorian Government's right to make regulations. Page A6.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
